channel.title: Curio Files
channel.description: True, faintly disgusting things from history, science and art. New file Monday, Wednesday, Saturday.

item.title: Monday, October 26
item.description:
Start small. That is the lesson today, and also the warning. Because the four smallest things in this episode, a spark, a snap, a smear of gold leaf, a single giggle, all turned into something nobody could stop once it got going.

item.title: Saturday, October 24
item.description: Some things just refuse to disappear. They get buried, bottled, scribbled on a napkin, or boiled off a dead man's hair, and centuries later they're still telling on us. Take San Francisco in 1859. item.title: Wednesday, October 21
item.description: There is a very specific kind of Tuesday where you get thrown out a castle window and somehow that is not the worst part of your week. That was Prague, May 1618. Two Catholic regents and their secretary got hauled to a high window of the castle by angry Protestant nobles and pitched out, seventy feet down, onto the rocks below. Except it wasn't rocks. item.title: Monday, October 19
item.description: Picture a factory floor in New Jersey, sometime around 1917. Rows of young women lean over watch faces under electric light, paintbrushes glowing a soft ghostly green between their fingers. The paint is radium, mixed in to make dials readable in the dark, and the trick to a fine line is simple, the company tells them, just touch the brush to your lips to bring it to a point. item.title: Tuesday, October 17
item.description: There is a particular kind of chaos that only happens when a body, or an army, decides to protect itself and gets it catastrophically wrong, and tonight's file is full of it. Start in the Romanian countryside in 1788, where the Austrian army is camped near a town called Karansebes, hunting Ottoman forces that are nowhere nearby. Some cavalry scouts cross a river, find a band of Roma traders sellin...

item.title: Wednesday, October 14
item.description: Picture a man who has conquered half of Europe, standing in a field, waiting for something small and fluffy to run away from him. That man is Napoleon Bonaparte, the year is 1807, and the something small is about to ruin his whole afternoon. His chief of staff had arranged a grand rabbit hunt to celebrate a treaty, and to make sure there would be plenty of rabbits, he ordered thousands of them fro...

item.title: Monday, October 12
item.description: Rome, January 897. The basilica smells like wax and something worse, because the guest of honor has been dead for nine months. Pope Formosus died quietly in bed, which should have been the end of it, but his successor Stephen the Sixth has other plans. item.title: Saturday, October 10
item.description: Boston, January 1919, unseasonably warm for January, which matters because warm weather makes molasses angrier than you'd think. A cast iron tank five stories tall, stuffed with over two million gallons of molasses meant for rum and munitions, had been groaning and leaking for years, workers used to scoop the drips into buckets and take them home as free syrup, nobody fixed the rivets. Then on Jan...

item.title: Wednesday, October 7
item.description: Strasbourg, July 1518. A woman named Frau Troffea steps into the street and starts to dance. Not a jig, not a celebration, just dancing, feet slamming the cobblestones, and she does not stop. A day passes. Then another. Within a month something like four hundred people have joined her, dancing through the summer heat with no music, no reason, some of them reportedly dying of heart attacks and stro...

item.title: Tuesday, October 6
item.description: In 1932 the government of Australia looked at a few thousand birds and decided the appropriate response was war. Western Australian wheat farmers were losing their crops to emus wandering in from the outback, so the Royal Australian Artillery sent Major Gwynydd Meredith and two Lewis machine guns to sort it out. The emus, it turned out, do not form neat lines for a firing squad. They scattered, zi...

item.title: Monday, October 5
item.description: There is a certain kind of story that only makes sense once you accept that humans and the universe both have a weakness for going way too far. Take London in 1888. Inside the Bryant and May match factory, teenage girls dipped matchsticks into white phosphorus all day, breathing fumes that crept into their jawbones and rotted them from the inside out. item.title: Saturday, October 3
item.description: Some stories are about things that go too far, too fast, and this is one of those days. Start in Stockholm harbor, 1628, where King Gustav II Adolf has just commissioned the fanciest warship Sweden has ever built. Two full gun decks. Gilded carvings crawling up the hull like a wedding cake designed by a general. The problem is nobody checked the math. The ship is top heavy, under ballasted, and pr...

item.title: Wednesday, September 30
item.description: In 1346 outside the stone walls of Caffa, a Genoese trading post on the Black Sea, the besieging Mongol army ran out of patience and arrows, so they started launching the dead instead. Soldiers dying of a horrific new plague, skin blackening, buboes swelling, were loaded onto catapults and hurled over the ramparts like the world's worst care package. item.title: Monday, September 28
item.description: London in the 1830s smelled of tallow candles and unwashed wool, and if you wanted a real night out, you didn't go to the opera, you went to see a dead Egyptian get undressed. Thomas Pettigrew, a surgeon who liked his science with a side of showbiz, would rent a hall, prop a three thousand year old body on a table, and start peeling. Tickets sold out. Ladies fainted, gentlemen took notes, and some...

item.title: Saturday, September 26
item.description: San Francisco, 1859. A failed rice speculator named Joshua Norton walks into a newspaper office and hands over a proclamation. He is no longer a bankrupt businessman. He is, effective immediately, Emperor of these United States. The city could have laughed him into the bay. Instead it played along for twenty one years, printing his own currency, seating him free at theaters, saluting him on the st...

item.title: Wednesday, September 23
item.description: Every good con starts with a small, believable lie, and 1920s New Jersey had a beauty. Girls barely out of school sat at long tables in the U.S. Radium Corporation, painting watch dials with glow in the dark paint made from actual radium. Their bosses taught them a trick to keep the brush tip fine, lip, dip, paint. Put the bristles in your mouth, dip in the radium paste, paint the numbers, repeat,...

item.title: Monday, September 21
item.description:
There is a particular kind of horror that comes from something familiar turning strange right in front of you. A brewery. A painting. A puddle of pond scum. A bucket of chowder. All ordinary, all hiding something you did not expect, and today they all get their moment.

item.title: Saturday, September 19
item.description:
Time is a liar, and nowhere does it lie harder than in the four scenes we're digging up today.
Start in Rome, January 897. Pope Formosus has been dead for nine months, buried, decomposing, doing what corpses do best. item.title: Wednesday, September 16
item.description: Every good disaster starts the same way, something gets bottled up until it can't be anymore. Boston, January 1919, the North End is stacked with tenements and a steel tank fifty feet tall, holding two point three million gallons of molasses meant for munitions and rum. item.title: Monday, September 14
item.description: Every good disaster starts with somebody deciding a bad idea is actually a great one. Strasbourg, July 1518, a woman named Frau Troffea steps into the street and starts dancing. Not fun dancing. Not wedding dancing. The kind of dancing where your feet bleed through your shoes and you keep going anyway. item.title: Saturday, September 12
item.description: Picture London in July of 1858, when the Thames stopped being a river and started being a punishment. Decades of raw sewage had baked in the summer heat until the smell rolled off the water like a physical wall. Members of Parliament, sitting right on the riverbank, soaked their curtains in chloride of lime and still gagged through debates. Newspapers called it the Great Stink, which undersells it...

item.title: Thursday, September 10
item.description:
